content: The study analyzed data from 118 participants across a single randomized controlled trial to evaluate the effectiveness of head and neck covers in reducing contamination during the doffing of personal protective equipment (PPE). The findings are as follows: 1. Anterior Neck Contamination: The use of a head and neck cover showed little to no difference in reducing small-sized contaminated patches (<1 cm²) on the anterior neck during PPE doffing. The median difference (MD) was 6 lower, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) indicating no significant improvement or worsening. The evidence quality was rated low due to serious indirectness and imprecision. 2. Posterior Neck Contamination: Similarly, the use of a head and neck cover demonstrated little to no difference in reducing small-sized contaminated patches (<1 cm²) on the posterior neck during PPE doffing. The MD was 5 lower, with a 95% CI showing no significant change. The evidence quality was again rated low due to serious indirectness and imprecision. 3. Hair and Head Contamination: The head and neck cover showed minimal impact on reducing small-sized contaminated patches (<1 cm²) on the hair and head during PPE doffing. The MD was 10 lower, with a 95% CI indicating no significant difference. The evidence quality was rated low due to serious indirectness and imprecision. 4. Overall Contamination: For overall contamination involving extra-large contaminated patches (≥5 cm²), the head and neck cover showed little to no difference during PPE doffing. The MD was 8 lower, with a 95% CI showing no significant change. The evidence quality was rated low due to serious indirectness and imprecision. 5. Anterior Neck Contamination with Extra-Large Patches: The use of a head and neck cover showed little to no difference in reducing extra-large contaminated patches (≥5 cm²) on the anterior neck during PPE doffing. The MD was 24 lower, with a 95% CI indicating no significant improvement. The evidence quality was rated low due to serious indirectness and imprecision. 6. Posterior Neck Contamination with Extra-Large Patches: The head and neck cover demonstrated little to no difference in reducing extra-large contaminated patches (≥5 cm²) on the posterior neck during PPE doffing. The MD was 24 lower, with a 95% CI showing no significant change. The evidence quality was rated low due to serious indirectness and imprecision. 7. Hair and Head Contamination with Extra-Large Patches: The head and neck cover showed minimal impact on reducing extra-large contaminated patches (≥5 cm²) on the hair and head during PPE doffing. The MD was 17 higher, with a 95% CI indicating no significant difference. The evidence quality was rated low due to serious indirectness and imprecision. Limitations of the Evidence: Risk of Bias: The study was downgraded due to concerns about allocation bias, lack of blinding of participants, and unclear reporting of all outcomes. Indirectness: The evidence was downgraded due to reliance on simulation studies using fluorescent contamination as a surrogate outcome, which may not fully represent real-world conditions for Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) or Marburg Virus Disease. Imprecision: The study had a small sample size, and the optimal information size (OIS) threshold was not met, leading to serious imprecision in the results. Publication Bias: No serious concerns were identified regarding publication bias. In conclusion, the use of head and neck covers during PPE doffing may not significantly reduce contamination, and the evidence is limited by methodological concerns and indirectness. Further research with larger sample sizes and real-world conditions is needed to draw more definitive conclusions.
